title: Schema evolution and encoding
subtitle: Change the shape of your data so that old code can read new data, and new code can read old data, while both run at once.

c.v: On 19 July 2024, Windows machines running CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor crashed. The cause was not new code. It was new data that the sensor code could not safely read.
In February 2024, sensor version 7.11 added a new template type for IPC (named pipes). Content files for it arrive from the cloud as Channel File 291.
Both parts were built at the same time, and they disagreed from day one. The template's definition said each check had 21 input fields. The sensor code supplied only 20.
For months, nobody noticed. The tests and the first live content used a wildcard for the 21st field, so the sensor never had to look at it.

Then two new content entries were sent. One had a real value for the 21st field. The content validator approved it, because it also assumed 21 inputs. The sensor tried to read input 21 from an array of 20. That out-of-bounds read crashed the system.

The data and the code that read it disagreed about the shape, and the code did not check the array size. Among its fixes, CrowdStrike now checks the number of fields when it builds the sensor. It also added a bounds check that runs on the machine.
This lesson is about that gap between writer and reader, and how data formats help you close it.
Every time you send or store data, you
encode
it into bytes. Later, some other code
decodes
it. That other code may be older or newer than the code that wrote it.
This happens all the time, not only in rare cases:
Rolling deploys
Kubernetes scales up the new pods while it scales down the old ones.
For a few minutes, v1 and v2 talk to each other.
Messages in a queue or log.
A message written yesterday by v1 is read today by v2. In a log, it may be read again in a year.
Stored data.
A database row or a file written three years ago is still read by today's code.
So you need two promises:
Backward compatibility
new code can read data written by old code.
Forward compatibility
old code can read data written by new code.
Forward is the harder one. Old code cannot know what you will add later. So it must be built to skip what it does not know.
The key idea.
Old and new code always overlap. Change your data so both can read it: add optional fields, never change the meaning of an existing one, and never reuse an old name or number.
JSON: no schema, so the rules live in your code
JSON carries field names, so a reader can find fields in any order. But nothing checks the shape. Two habits keep JSON safe:
Ignore unknown fields.
Then new fields do not break old readers. Some parsers reject them by default. ProtoJSON parsers do, for example.
Check yours.
Treat missing fields as normal.
Then new readers can read old data.
Numbers are a trap. RFC 8259 lets parsers limit precision. Only integers between −(2^53 − 1) and 2^53 − 1 are safe to exchange.
JavaScript stores every number as a double, so bigger integers get rounded.

blocks.v:
JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}').id
// 9007199254740992 — a different id, and no error

c.v: Send big ids, such as 64-bit database keys, as strings.
Protobuf
's own JSON format does this for all 64-bit integers, for the same reason.
Protocol Buffers: the field number is the contract
In Protobuf, each field has a
field number
. The bytes on the wire carry that number, not the field name. So you can rename a field, but you can never change its number.
Later, when no reader needs field 2, v3 deletes it and adds
reserved 2;
and
reserved "amount";
The rules that matter:
Adding and removing fields is safe.
Changing a field's number is not.
Never reuse a number.
Google's guide says it "messes up deserialization". When you delete a field, reserve its number.
Also reserve the name, so no new field reuses it. JSON and text formats carry names, not numbers.
Unknown fields survive.
An old proto3 reader keeps fields it does not know, and writes them out again.
They are lost if you convert the message to JSON.
Missing means default.
A missing string reads as empty, a number as zero, and a bool as false.
So "zero" and "not sent" look the same.
Use
optional
when "not sent" matters.
Then you can check whether a value was set.
Do not change a field's type.
A few types are wire-compatible, such as
int32
and
int64
. But a big value read as
int32
is cut short with no error.
No required fields.
Proto3 has none. In proto2, never add one.
Step through a rolling deploy that shares one queue. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.
Avro: the reader needs the writer's schema
Avro
has no field numbers. Binary Avro data has no field names or types either. So a reader needs the exact schema the data was written with: the
writer's schema
The reader also has its own schema, the
reader's schema
. Avro matches the two by field name.
A field only in the writer's schema is ignored.
A field only in the reader's schema takes its default.
If that field has no default, the read fails.
So if both old and new readers must work, add or remove only fields that have a default.
In Avro before 1.12, a union default had to match the first type in the union. Version 1.12 accepts the first type that matches.
Many tools still use the old rule, so put
"null"
first when the default is null.
Where does the writer's schema come from? An Avro file stores it once in its header.
For records stored one by one, such as rows in a database, each record carries a schema version or id. A
schema registry
maps that id to the full schema.
With Confluent Schema Registry, each Kafka message begins with a version byte and a 4-byte schema ID.
Schema registries and compatibility modes
A registry also guards changes. Confluent Schema Registry checks each new schema against old ones before it accepts it.
BACKWARD
(the default): consumers on the new schema can read data written with the last schema. Upgrade consumers first.
FORWARD
: consumers on the old schema can read data written with the new schema. Upgrade producers first. Then make sure consumers no longer read old data.
FULL
: both. You can upgrade either side in any order.
Each mode also has a
_TRANSITIVE
form. It checks against all older schemas, not only the last one.
Confluent made BACKWARD the default so that consumers can rewind to the start of a topic.
If your topic keeps data for a long time, a transitive mode is safer.
What no format can catch
Every check above looks at names, numbers and types. None of them looks at meaning. Say you keep
int64 amount = 2
, but start to send paise instead of rupees. The schema is the same, so every check passes. Old readers now show prices 100 times too high.
So a change of unit or meaning is a new field, with a new name and a new number. That is why the example above added
amount_paise
instead of changing
amount
JSON
Names are in the data.
, if readers ignore unknown fields.
Nothing checks shape. Big numbers lose precision.
Public APIs, webhooks, browsers.
Protobuf
, to know names. Unknown fields can still be skipped.
Old code skips them.
A reused field number gives wrong data, silently.
Calls between your own services, such as gRPC.
Avro
The exact writer's schema.
Old readers ignore it. A default lets new readers read old data.
Lost or wrong writer's schema means unreadable data.
Kafka topics and data files, with a registry.
Simple rule:
pick the format your readers can handle. Then put a compatibility check in
CI
, not in a reviewer's memory.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: For every data change, ask:
"Who reads this, and how old can their code be?"
Count queue backlog, log retention and stored rows, not only live services.
Add new fields as optional, with a safe default. Never make a new field required.
Never change the meaning or unit of a field. To move from rupees to paise, add
amount_paise
and keep
amount
until nobody reads it.
Deprecate
before you delete. Stop writing the field, wait until no reader needs it, then delete it and reserve its number and name.
Run a schema check in CI. For Protobuf, a breaking-change
linter
. For Kafka, the registry's compatibility mode.
Make readers fail safe on bad input. CrowdStrike's fix was a bounds check at runtime as well as a check at build time.
For changes to public HTTP APIs, use
API versioning and lifecycle
. For database columns, use
zero-downtime schema migrations
"Compare this .proto file with the one on main. List every change that breaks old readers or old writers: changed or reused field numbers, changed types, removed fields without
reserved
, and new required fields."
"Here is our Avro schema and the new version. Would Confluent Schema Registry accept it in BACKWARD mode? In FORWARD mode? Explain each field."
"Find every place our JavaScript code parses JSON ids that can be larger than 2^53 − 1. Change them to strings end to end."
No field number was reused or renumbered. An agent may "tidy up" numbers so they run 1, 2, 3.
Every deleted Protobuf field has its number and name in
reserved
Every new Avro field has a default, and a union default matches the first type, for older Avro tools.
No field kept its name but changed its unit or meaning. A linter cannot catch that.
The plan says which side deploys first, and it matches the registry mode.
Queues vs logs
: why old messages stay around to be read again.
Webhooks and async APIs
: JSON events that your customers decode with code you cannot update.
Safe deploys and config changes
: rolling out content and config as carefully as code.
Kafka internals
: how the messages you encode are stored and replicated.
Coming later: RPC and
gRPC
, and contract and
integration tests

q.v: A rolling deploy is half done. New pods write messages with a new field. Old pods still read from the same queue. Which property must the format give you?

options.v: Backward compatibility, so new code can read old data.
Forward compatibility, so old code can read data written by new code.
Neither. A queue keeps the versions apart.

why.v: Old readers meet data from a newer writer. That is forward compatibility. The queue does not keep the versions apart.

q.v: . What happens to services that still run the old code?

options.v: They fail to parse the message and log an error.
They read the discount value as the amount, with no error.
They skip field 2, because its name changed.

why.v: The wire format carries only the number and the value, not the name. Old code still maps number 2 to amount. Reserve deleted numbers so this cannot happen.

q.v: In Avro, a new reader's schema adds a field
with no default. It reads a record written with the old schema. What happens?

options.v: The field is set to null.
The field is set to an empty string.

why.v: The Avro spec says that if the reader's field has no default and the writer's schema lacks it, an error is signalled.

q.v: A JavaScript service parses the JSON

options.v: An error, because the number is too big.

why.v: JavaScript numbers are doubles. Integers above 2^53 − 1 cannot all be stored exactly, so the value is rounded with no error.

q.v: Your topic uses Confluent Schema Registry with the default BACKWARD mode. You delete a field that has no default. What should you upgrade first?

options.v: Order does not matter in BACKWARD mode.

why.v: Confluent's docs say that for BACKWARD, you upgrade all consumers before you start producing new events.
